assignments.reason: Mishpat (self-judgment) belongs by essential nature to the domain of din/yirah. The Torah defines it as 'מַה שֶּׁהָאָדָם שׁוֹפֵט וְדָן עַצְמוֹ' — a person judging himself. Judgment (din) is structurally the same force as fear (yirah): both are expressions of gevurah/strict justice. The Torah explicitly links mishpat to eretz/yirah via the verse 'מֶלֶךְ בְּמִשְׁפָּט יַעֲמִיד אֶרֶץ'. Mishpat is the holy, self-directed form of din — it is judgment channeled positively, hence polarity good.

assignments.node_id: מה שהוא בעצמו שופט את עצמו
assignments.reason: This is the concrete enactment of mishpat — the person actively judging himself. By essential nature it is the same concept-domain as mishpat: self-directed din, which is the holy expression of the gevurah/judgment force. It belongs to the yirah-domain because self-judgment is the internalized form of the same strict-justice quality that yirah embodies. Polarity good because it represents the person proactively exercising holy judgment on himself before Heaven does.

Being saved from heavenly judgment belongs by essential nature to the domain of din/yirah. It is the state where heavenly din is nullified — the positive resolution of the entire judgment/fear axis. The Torah states: 'כְּשֶׁיֵּשׁ דִּין לְמַטָּה אֵין דִּין לְמַעְלָה' — when judgment exists below, there is no judgment above. This removal of upper din is what allows yirah to stop falling and to remain in its elevated state (יִרְאַת הָרוֹמְמוּת). The concept is inherently about the nullification of din, placing it squarely in the yirah/din domain. Polarity good because it is the desired holy outcome — freedom from punitive judgment.
